episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Tuesday, May twelfth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off today's Innovation Pulse, career and technical education is seeing a significant surge in student interest. Education Week reports K-12 C.T.E. participation rose roughly ten percent between the 2022-23 and 2023-24 school years, from about 7.8 million to 8.6 million students, according to the U.S. Department of Education. Seventy-one percent of pre-college educators surveyed say student interest in C.T.E. has increased over the past five years. Among fields expected to see the most growth, thirty-one percent of educators selected digital, A.I., and cybersecurity offerings, followed by construction and advanced manufacturing at eighteen percent each. School districts are expanding C.T.E. offerings to meet demand, and industry partnerships are driving curriculum development, with employers directly involved in designing programs that address real workforce needs. The trend is fueled by students and parents increasingly questioning the return on investment of traditional four-year college degrees while seeking programs that offer both immediate job prospects and pathways to further education.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to graduate perspectives, despite growing fears about how artificial intelligence will disrupt the job market, American college and university alumni say that earning a college degree is still as important as it was twenty years ago. The Lumina Foundation-Gallup survey of nearly six thousand two- and four-year degree holders found that seventy-one percent of all surveyed alumni said their education was worth the price they paid for it. Asked if they would do it again, ninety-three percent said yes. More than three-quarters of bachelor's degree holders and fifty-two percent of associate degree holders said their degree was critical or important to reaching their financial goals. However, only one in ten bachelor's degree graduates said that four-year colleges charge a fair price for what they offer. Half of all student loan borrowers reported delaying at least one significant life event because of their loans.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile at institutions nationwide, A.I. literacy belongs in required first-year college programs to ensure all students gain essential understanding before academic paths diverge. That's the argument from Agnes Scott College president Leocadia Zak, writing in Times Higher Education. Beginning this fall, Agnes Scott will embed A.I. education in its existing first-year experience program rather than creating separate requirements. The curriculum focuses on three core areas: conceptual understanding of how A.I. systems function, ethical reasoning about bias and societal impacts, and practical application in professional contexts. This foundation prepares students for discipline-specific A.I. engagement in later coursework while establishing common frameworks for responsible use. First-year integration ensures students develop critical evaluation skills before A.I. tools become normalized in their academic work.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In program development news, Michigan State University debuts an online master's program combining educational statistics with A.I. applications. The Educational Statistics and A.I. program launches Fall 2026 to train educators, researchers, and administrators in data science and A.I. specifically for educational settings. Program coordinator Porsche Fischer describes it as the natural next step in M.S.U.'s and the College of Education's A.I. leadership. The degree builds on the college's established Measurement and Quantitative Methods Ph.D. program. Faculty includes world-renowned scholars who lead the college's successful doctoral programs in quantitative methods. The online format allows working educators to pursue advanced training without leaving their positions.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And in workforce data, machine learning expertise leads demand in A.I.-related job postings across the United States job market. Statista data shows machine learning capabilities are the most sought-after qualification in A.I. positions, reflecting the technology's central role in business applications. Natural language processing ranks as the second most in-demand skill, driven by widespread adoption of conversational A.I. systems. Computer vision capabilities also show strong demand growth, particularly in manufacturing, healthcare, and autonomous systems development. The skills gap appears most pronounced in roles requiring both technical A.I. competency and domain expertise in specific industries. Employers increasingly seek professionals who can bridge A.I. capabilities with practical business applications rather than purely theoretical knowledge.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
